Introduction to the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel Model

dnsr package

2026-10-11

Source: vignettes/dns-model-introduction.Rmd
dns-model-introduction.Rmd

Overview

The dnsr package implements the Dynamic Nelson-Siegel (DNS) model for yield curve modelling. This vignette covers the workflow: fitting the curve, estimating how its factors move, simulating forward, and pricing off the result.

Everything here runs against treasury_yields, a six-year panel of real U.S. Treasury curves that ships with the package, so none of it needs a FRED API key. For live data see vignette("fred-api-setup", package = "dnsr"), and for the YUIMA simulation engine see vignette("dnsr-yuima-integration", package = "dnsr").

library(dnsr)
data(treasury_yields)

dim(treasury_yields)
#> [1] 1501   12
range(treasury_yields$Date)
#> [1] "2019-01-02" "2024-12-31"

The frame is the shape every function in the package expects: a Date column followed by one column per maturity, named by maturity in years, with yields in decimal form.

treasury_yields[1:3, 1:6]
#>         Date 0.0833   0.25    0.5      1      2
#> 1 2019-01-02 0.0240 0.0242 0.0251 0.0260 0.0250
#> 2 2019-01-03 0.0242 0.0241 0.0247 0.0250 0.0239
#> 3 2019-01-04 0.0240 0.0242 0.0251 0.0257 0.0250

The Nelson-Siegel Model

The Nelson-Siegel model is a parsimonious parametric model for the yield curve. It expresses the yield at each maturity through three factors:

y(m)=β1+β2(1−e−λmλm)+β3(1−e−λmλm−e−λm)y(m) = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m}\right) + \beta_3 \left(\frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m} - e^{-\lambda m}\right)

where

  • y(m)y(m) is the yield at maturity mm,
  • β1\beta_1 is the long-term level of interest rates,
  • β2\beta_2 is the slope, short-term minus long-term,
  • β3\beta_3 is the curvature, the size of the hump,
  • λ\lambda controls how fast the factor loadings decay.

The loadings are what give each factor its interpretation: the level loads equally on every maturity, the slope loads most at the short end and decays to zero, and the curvature peaks somewhere in the middle.

The units of lambda

λ\lambda appears only as the product λm\lambda m, so it is measured per unit of maturity. Its numerical value therefore depends on whether maturities are years or months, and a λ\lambda quoted on its own does not say which. Every function in this package takes maturities in years.

Diebold and Li chose λ=0.0609\lambda = 0.0609 working in months, where it places the curvature hump just short of 30 months. Against maturities in years the same number places it elsewhere:

ns_curvature_peak(0.0609)   # where the hump sits, in the maturity's own units
#> [1] 29.44634

Twenty-nine years, beyond the end of most curves, where the curvature loading is close to flat. ns_lambda() maps in the other direction, from a hump maturity to the decay that places it there:

ns_lambda(2.5)   # a hump at two and a half years
#> [1] 0.7173128
ns_lambda(30)    # the Diebold-Li criterion, in the months they worked in
#> [1] 0.05977607

0.0609 is therefore correct for month-denominated maturities and incorrect for maturities in years. The package default is ns_lambda(3.5), a hump at three and a half years, near the middle of a Treasury curve. The two loadings:

plot_dns_loadings(lambda = 0.0609)

plot_dns_loadings(lambda = ns_lambda(2.5))

The first has no hump within thirty years. The second has the shape the three-factor description implies.

The consequence is in the fit, not only the picture. At λ=0.0609\lambda = 0.0609 the slope loading falls from 0.992 at three months to 0.749 at ten years, which is close to the level loading of 1 at every maturity. The two factors are then nearly collinear and not separately identified, and β2\beta_2 no longer behaves like a slope. Fitting the same panel both ways and comparing β2\beta_2 with the quoted spread:

λ\lambda hump at cor(β2\beta_2, 3m-10y) same sign median fit
0.0609 29.4 y -0.928 5% 23.0 bp
0.448 4.0 y +0.941 90% 5.3 bp

At the month-denominated value the slope factor is negatively correlated with the spread and carries the same sign on 5 percent of dates. dnsr therefore does not use 0.0609 as its default.

Two qualifications on ns_lambda(). The curvature peak is flat: at half or double the nominal peak maturity the loading is still about 85 percent of its maximum, so λ\lambda is not tightly determined by this choice and the precision of the returned number overstates what it fixes. And λ\lambda also sets the decay of the slope loading, which is often the larger effect: a hump at 2.5 years leaves the slope loading at 0.53 by two years, a hump at 10 years leaves it at 0.84. Estimate λ\lambda where that is possible.

Dynamic Extension

The DNS model lets the three factors vary over time, each as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process:

dβi(t)=κi(θi−βi(t))dt+σidWi(t)d\beta_i(t) = \kappa_i(\theta_i - \beta_i(t))dt + \sigma_i dW_i(t)

with κi\kappa_i the speed of mean reversion, θi\theta_i the long-run mean, σi\sigma_i the volatility and Wi(t)W_i(t) a Wiener process. Fitting the curve is therefore two steps: a cross-sectional fit on each date, then a time-series estimate of how the resulting factors move.

Fitting a Single Curve

fit_ns_model() fits one cross-section. The default "profile" method solves the three betas in closed form at each λ\lambda and searches only over λ\lambda, so it needs no starting values for them:

maturities <- as.numeric(setdiff(names(treasury_yields), "Date"))
latest <- as.numeric(treasury_yields[nrow(treasury_yields), -1])

curve <- fit_ns_model(maturities, latest)
curve
#> Nelson-Siegel curve fit
#>   beta1 (level)     0.04927
#>   beta2 (slope)     -0.00515
#>   beta3 (curvature) -0.01551
#>   lambda            0.66877
#>   rmse              4.43 bp over 11 maturities

The fit reports whether any parameter came to rest on one of its bounds. A clamped fit can have a low RMSE while the factor decomposition is not identified, and a bounded optimiser reports convergence at a bound, so success alone does not distinguish the two:

curve$at_bound
#>  beta1  beta2  beta3 lambda 
#>  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE

Nothing is clamped here. Imposing the ceiling of 0.5 used before version 0.6.0 clamps this curve, which fits a faster decay than that allows:

pinched <- fit_ns_model(maturities, latest,
                        upper_bounds = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
#> Warning in fit_ns_model(maturities, latest, upper_bounds = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.5, :
#> Nelson-Siegel fit rests on a parameter bound (lambda); the factor decomposition
#> is not identified. Widen lower_bounds/upper_bounds or check the yield scale.
c(lambda = pinched$parameters[["lambda"]], rmse_bp = pinched$rmse * 10000)
#>   lambda  rmse_bp 
#> 0.500000 4.948436
pinched$at_bound
#>  beta1  beta2  beta3 lambda 
#>  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE

The clamped fit returns λ\lambda exactly on 0.5 with a higher error, and flags it through at_bound.

Fitting the Panel

fit_dns_model() fits every date. The window is selected by date, so it does not matter which row order the panel arrives in.

A panel raises a choice that a single curve does not. If λ\lambda is estimated freely it varies from date to date, on this data from 0.17 to 2.00, the ceiling. β2\beta_2 then multiplies a differently shaped loading at each date, so the betas are not a comparable time series, which is what the next step requires.

Standard DNS practice, following Diebold and Li, therefore fixes λ\lambda at a single value for the whole panel. The cost is cross-sectional fit, about 6.4 basis points median here against 4.5 with λ\lambda free; the gain is factors that are comparable across dates and can be modelled over time.

ns_lambda(4) places the curvature hump at four years, close to the panel optimum, and keeps the loadings distinct:

recent <- fit_dns_model(treasury_yields, n_days = 250, show_progress = FALSE,
                        lambda_constraint = "fixed",
                        initial_lambda = ns_lambda(4))
recent
#> Dynamic Nelson-Siegel fit
#>   250 curves, 2024-01-02 to 2024-12-31
#>   maturities         0.0833  0.2500  0.5000  1.0000  2.0000  3.0000  5.0000  7.0000 10.0000 20.0000 30.0000
#>   rmse              5.28 bp median, 12.08 bp worst
#>   lambda            0.4483 median
#>   success rate      100.0%

summary() gives the distribution of each factor and of the fit error:

summary(recent)
#> Dynamic Nelson-Siegel fit
#>   250 curves, 2024-01-02 to 2024-12-31, 100.0% fitted
#> 
#> Factors:
#>             min     mean      max      sd
#> beta1   0.04314  0.04649  0.05018 0.00135
#> beta2  -0.00663  0.00680  0.01352 0.00484
#> beta3  -0.04877 -0.02768 -0.00824 0.01029
#> lambda  0.44832  0.44832  0.44832 0.00000
#> 
#> Fit error (basis points):
#>    0%   50%   95%  100% 
#>  3.43  5.28 10.24 12.08

Fitted curves against the observations:

plot_yield_curves(treasury_yields, recent, max_plots = 4)

And the factors over time:

factor_plots <- plot_factor_time_series(recent)
factor_plots$factors

factor_plots$rmse

Checking the factor interpretation

The three factors are described as level, slope and curvature. Each claim is testable. The slope factor should track the quoted spread:

aligned <- treasury_yields[match(recent$parameters$Date, treasury_yields$Date), ]
observed_spread <- aligned[["0.25"]] - aligned[["10"]]

c(
  correlation = cor(recent$parameters$beta2, observed_spread),
  same_sign = mean(sign(recent$parameters$beta2) == sign(observed_spread))
)
#> correlation   same_sign 
#>   0.9410156   0.9040000

The correlation is high and the sign follows from the loadings: the slope loading is 1 at the short end and decays to zero, so y(short)≈β1+β2y(\text{short}) \approx \beta_1 + \beta_2 and y(long)≈β1y(\text{long}) \approx \beta_1, making β2\beta_2 the short-minus-long spread. A positive β2\beta_2 corresponds to an inverted curve.

The level factor tracks the policy cycle:

range(recent$parameters$beta1)
#> [1] 0.04314019 0.05018226

Residuals by maturity

The median fit error summarises the residuals; their distribution across maturities is more informative. Three factors constrain the shapes the curve can take:

fitted_rows <- recent$fitted_yields
residual <- as.matrix(aligned[, -1]) - fitted_rows

data.frame(
  maturity = as.numeric(colnames(fitted_rows)),
  mean_bp = round(colMeans(residual, na.rm = TRUE) * 10000, 1),
  rmse_bp = round(sqrt(colMeans(residual^2, na.rm = TRUE)) * 10000, 1)
)
#>        maturity mean_bp rmse_bp
#> 0.0833   0.0833     0.1     7.9
#> 0.25     0.2500     3.3     5.0
#> 0.5      0.5000     1.1     6.1
#> 1        1.0000    -4.7     8.5
#> 2        2.0000    -2.7     5.5
#> 3        3.0000    -0.5     1.9
#> 5        5.0000     1.5     4.3
#> 7        7.0000     3.1     5.0
#> 10      10.0000    -1.2     3.2
#> 20      20.0000     8.6     8.7
#> 30      30.0000    -8.7     9.4

The errors are not uniform across maturities. The middle of the curve, where the curvature loading is largest, fits to a few basis points. Both ends are three to five times worse, and the long end shows a systematic pattern: twenty years is fitted low and thirty high, which is what a single exponential decay produces on a curve that flattens faster than it can represent. The one-month point has a different cause: it is not well described by the same curve as the rest, and no three-factor shape fits both the bill market and the thirty-year point.

Which maturities matter depends on the application. For discounting long cashflows, the median RMSE is not the relevant summary.

Estimating Factor Dynamics

estimate_dns_dynamics() regresses each factor’s change on its lagged level. By default it samples the factor series at month-ends and estimates at Δt=1/12\Delta t = 1/12. Daily cross-sectional refits carry serially uncorrelated measurement noise, and an OU regression on daily changes attributes that noise to mean reversion, inflating κ\kappa by about an order of magnitude.

Since the estimation uses month-ends, fitting only those is sufficient and faster. warm_start = FALSE makes each cross-section independent of the other dates in the panel, so these fits match what fitting every day would produce:

month_ends <- treasury_yields[
  !duplicated(format(treasury_yields$Date, "%Y-%m"), fromLast = TRUE),
]
monthly_fit <- fit_dns_model(month_ends, n_days = nrow(month_ends),
                             show_progress = FALSE, warm_start = FALSE,
                             lambda_constraint = "fixed",
                             initial_lambda = ns_lambda(4))

dynamics <- estimate_dns_dynamics(monthly_fit$parameters)
dynamics
#> DNS factor dynamics
#>   estimated on     2019-02-28 to 2024-12-31
#>   sampling         monthly (dt = 1/12), 71 observations
#>   structure        diagonal
#> 
#>                 kappa se_kappa   theta  sigma half_life_y
#> level (b1)     0.0604   0.3378  0.0862 0.0088     11.4681
#> slope (b2)     0.3534   0.3484 -0.0058 0.0114      1.9615
#> curvature (b3) 1.5240   0.7039 -0.0150 0.0306      0.4548
#> 
#>   stable           TRUE (eigenvalues 1.524 0.353 0.060)

Mean reversion is weakly determined in a sample this short. The standard errors and the half-life interval show the range involved:

dynamics$beta1$se
#>        kappa        theta        sigma 
#> 0.3378346439 0.3155525922 0.0007481728
dynamics$beta1$t_value
#>     kappa     theta 
#> 0.1789075 0.2731285
dynamics$beta1$half_life_ci
#>     lower     upper 
#> 0.9592606       Inf

κ\kappa also carries an upward small-sample bias of order 5/T5/T in a sample of TT years. The standard errors above measure sampling noise, not that bias.

Factor innovations are correlated, and the simulation uses the correlation:

round(dynamics$correlation, 3)
#>        beta1  beta2  beta3
#> beta1  1.000 -0.548  0.132
#> beta2 -0.548  1.000 -0.302
#> beta3  0.132 -0.302  1.000

A full mean-reversion matrix

By default the three factors revert independently. structure = "full" estimates the Diebold-Li VAR(1) instead, in which a shock to one factor affects the others:

full <- estimate_dns_dynamics(monthly_fit$parameters, structure = "full")
round(full$kappa_matrix, 3)
#>        beta1  beta2  beta3
#> beta1  0.436 -0.494 -0.391
#> beta2 -1.190  0.866 -0.843
#> beta3  0.921  0.635  1.675

The eigenvalues of that matrix determine whether the system is stable. A diagonal reconstruction gives a different answer when the cross terms are non-negligible:

round(Re(full$eigenvalues), 3)
#> [1] 1.176 1.176 0.626
full$system_stability
#> [1] TRUE

Diagnostics

The package reports fit diagnostics across several objects:

# 1. Did every cross-section fit at all?
recent$success_rate
#> [1] 100
nrow(recent$failures)
#> [1] 0

# 2. Did any fit come to rest on a bound? Those factor decompositions are not
#    identified, however good their RMSE looks.
colSums(recent$at_bound)
#>  beta1  beta2  beta3 lambda 
#>      0      0      0      0

# 3. How bad is the worst curve, not just the median?
round(quantile(recent$parameters$rmse * 10000, c(0.5, 0.95, 1)), 2)
#>   50%   95%  100% 
#>  5.28 10.24 12.08

# 4. Is the estimated factor system actually mean reverting?
dynamics$system_stability
#> [1] TRUE
round(Re(dynamics$eigenvalues), 3)
#> [1] 1.524 0.353 0.060

# 5. How well identified is the reversion speed?
dynamics$beta1$half_life_ci
#>     lower     upper 
#> 0.9592606       Inf

What to look for: a high success rate with no bound hits, an acceptable worst-case RMSE, a stable system, and a finite half-life interval. If the half-life interval runs to infinity, as it does on this six-year sample, κ\kappa is not determined by the data, and a simulation horizon longer than the sample extrapolates beyond what was estimated.

Simulating Future Yield Curves

The factor system is a linear SDE whose diffusion does not depend on the state, so its transition law over any step is a known Gaussian. engine = "exact" samples that law directly, which carries no discretisation error at any step size and needs no additional package.

latest_row <- monthly_fit$parameters[which.max(monthly_fit$parameters$Date), ]
initial_factors <- as.numeric(latest_row[c("beta1", "beta2", "beta3")])

sim_params <- dns_dynamics_to_sim_params(dynamics, lambda = latest_row$lambda)

simulation <- simulate_dns_yield_curves(
  params = sim_params,
  initial_factors = initial_factors,
  maturities = maturities,
  time_horizon = 5,
  n_steps = 60,
  n_paths = 500,
  engine = "exact",
  seed = 1
)
simulation
#> DNS simulation
#>   500 paths, 60 steps over 5 years
#>   engine           exact
#>   terminal factors 0.0597  -0.0065  -0.0145
#>     (sd)           0.0177  0.0135  0.0173
#>   maturities        0.0833  0.2500  0.5000  1.0000  2.0000  3.0000  5.0000  7.0000 10.0000 20.0000 30.0000
#>   terminal yields  5.30  5.27  5.24  5.19  5.18  5.21  5.33  5.44  5.57  5.77  5.83 (% mean)

Simulated curves at a few horizons. The facets follow the calendar rather than sorting lexically, so “Year 5” comes after “Year 3”:

yield_plots <- plot_simulated_yields(
  simulation,
  time_points = c(0, 1, 3, 5),
  path_subset = 1:5
)
yield_plots$yield_curves

The factor paths, as a fan of quantiles across all 500 of them:

plot_simulated_factors(simulation)$level

The YUIMA engine remains available and is the default, for the estimation functions it provides. See vignette("dnsr-yuima-integration", package = "dnsr").

Pricing off a Fitted Curve

The DNS curve gives continuously compounded zero rates, so the discount factor at maturity mm is P(m)=exp⁡(−y(m)m)P(m) = \exp(-y(m)\,m):

factors <- matrix(curve$parameters[1:3], nrow = 1)
lambda <- curve$parameters[["lambda"]]

coupon_maturities <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 30)
data.frame(
  maturity = coupon_maturities,
  zero_pct = round(calculate_dns_yields(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ] * 100, 3),
  discount = round(dns_discount_factors(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ], 4),
  price_100 = round(dns_zero_prices(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ], 2),
  par_pct = round(dns_par_yields(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ] * 100, 3)
)
#>   maturity zero_pct discount price_100 par_pct
#> 1      0.5    4.282   0.9788     97.88   4.328
#> 2      1.0    4.216   0.9587     95.87   4.261
#> 3      2.0    4.196   0.9195     91.95   4.240
#> 4      5.0    4.386   0.8031     80.31   4.423
#> 5     10.0    4.621   0.6300     63.00   4.639
#> 6     30.0    4.824   0.2352     23.52   4.812

Par yields are the coupon rate that prices a bullet bond at par. They differ from zero yields for two reasons with opposite signs: a compounding term, since the curve is continuously compounded while the par rate pays semi-annually, and a shape term, since coupons are discounted at the earlier rates rather than the terminal one. The compounding term dominates at the short end, the shape term further out.

Forward rates come off the same factors:

rbind(
  spot = round(calculate_dns_yields(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ] * 100, 3),
  forward = round(calculate_dns_forwards(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)[1, ] * 100, 3)
)
#>          [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]  [,5]  [,6]
#> spot    4.282 4.216 4.196 4.386 4.621 4.824
#> forward 4.188 4.132 4.248 4.726 4.914 4.927

Looking at the Panel

A heatmap of the whole panel shows the 2020 collapse to near-zero short rates and the 2022-2023 inversion:

plot_yield_heatmap(treasury_yields)

Principal components of the daily changes. Decomposing the covariance matrix rather than standardising each maturity first is the usual convention for yield curves, and produces the level, slope and curvature shapes:

pca <- plot_yield_pca(treasury_yields, scale = FALSE)
round(pca$var_explained[1:3], 4)
#> [1] 0.7160 0.1087 0.0991
pca$plots$weights

The first three components are the empirical counterpart of the model’s three factors.

Comparing Term Structure Models

compare_term_structure_models() fits several curves to one cross-section and reports the error of each, in basis points:

comparison <- compare_term_structure_models(
  treasury_yields,
  models = c("NS", "NSS", "Spline")
)
comparison$metrics
#>                    Model     RMSE      MAE  MaxError
#> 1          Nelson-Siegel 4.431432 3.887569  8.700489
#> 2 Nelson-Siegel-Svensson 3.542643 2.502529  8.621915
#> 3           Cubic Spline 5.561295 3.995767 11.985578
comparison$plot

Nelson-Siegel-Svensson adds a second curvature term with its own decay. It nests Nelson-Siegel and so cannot fit worse in sample, at the cost of two further parameters. A smoothing spline usually has a lower in-sample error than either and imposes no shape, so its parameters do not carry an interpretation.

One-Step Estimation

Everything above estimates in two steps: each cross-section is fitted, and the resulting factors are then treated as data for a time-series model. The factors are estimates carrying sampling error, and using them as observed biases κ\kappa upward.

estimate_dns_state_space() estimates the same model in one step, as the state-space system of Diebold, Rudebusch and Aruoba, by maximum likelihood with a Kalman filter. The factors become an unobserved state, their measurement uncertainty enters the likelihood, λ\lambda is estimated jointly with the dynamics, and missing maturities are handled by shrinking the measurement equation for that date.

one_step <- estimate_dns_state_space(treasury_yields,
                                     lambda = ns_lambda(3.5),
                                     measurement = "common")
one_step
#> DNS one-step state-space fit (Kalman filter, maximum likelihood)
#>   estimated on     2019-01-31 to 2024-12-31
#>   sampling         monthly (dt = 1/11.8), 72 dates, 11 maturities
#>   lambda           0.5124 fixed (hump at 3.50 years)
#> 
#>                 kappa   theta  sigma half_life_y
#> level (b1)     0.1214  0.0365 0.0078      5.7109
#> slope (b2)     0.4663 -0.0034 0.0109      1.4865
#> curvature (b3) 0.4533 -0.0160 0.0259      1.5291
#> 
#>   measurement sd   13.37 bp median across maturities
#>   fit              11.92 bp rmse
#>   logLik           3863.72 on 13 parameters (AIC -7701.4, BIC -7640.7)
#>   stable           TRUE
#>   $two_step holds the two-step estimates used as starting values

The smoothed factors have the same shape as the two-step parameters frame, and summary() reports both sets side by side:

head(one_step$factors)
#>         Date      beta1        beta2       beta3
#> 1 2019-01-31 0.03007925 -0.005008562 -0.01156606
#> 2 2019-02-28 0.03077127 -0.005530049 -0.01055434
#> 3 2019-03-29 0.02872613 -0.003504591 -0.01647100
#> 4 2019-04-30 0.02929922 -0.003959725 -0.01651064
#> 5 2019-05-31 0.02671109 -0.001949996 -0.02249331
#> 6 2019-06-28 0.02555954 -0.002923954 -0.02310094

The costs are run time, needing the whole panel at once, and a harder numerical problem. There is also a limit on what either estimator determines: λ\lambda, the shock volatilities and the measurement error are recovered precisely, but κ\kappa and θ\theta are not well determined at realistic sample lengths. ?estimate_dns_state_space gives the measured errors from simulated data.

The factor system here is diagonal. For a full mean-reversion matrix, use estimate_dns_dynamics(structure = "full") on two-step betas.

What This Package Does Not Do

It carries no arbitrage-free restriction. Nelson-Siegel is a flexible curve rather than a term structure model derived from a no-arbitrage condition, so a fitted or simulated curve can imply arbitrage. The arbitrage-free variant, AFNS, adds a yield-adjustment term that ties the dynamics and the cross-section together. The distinction matters for pricing derivatives off these curves, less so for discounting cashflows.

get_calibrated_dns_params() wraps the two-step path above into one call, from downloading data to returning simulation-ready parameters, for when the intermediate objects are not needed.
